subtitle: Three quick checks — a concept question, an explanation, and a coding challenge. Each submit saves here and Claude picks it up in the chat.

mc.prompt: A sorted array has $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ elements. Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case?
mc.explainCorrect: Right — each comparison halves the remaining search space, so it takes about $\log_2(1{,}000{,}000) \approx 20$ steps, not a fraction of $n$.
mc.explainWrong: Not quite — binary search halves the search space every comparison. Halving repeatedly is what $\log_2 n$ measures: $\log_2(1{,}000{,}000) \approx 20$.

free.prompt: In your own words: why does cutting the search space in half each step give $O(\log_2 n)$ time, rather than $O(n)$?

code.promptHTML: Implement binarySearch(arr, target): return the index of target in the sorted array arr, or -1 if it isn't present. Aim for $O(\log n)$, not a linear scan.
